clue.text: Senior relative (female) to be facing both ways

definitions.text: Senior relative (female) to be facing both ways

parts.words: Senior relative (female) to be facing both ways
parts.note: a senior female relative is an Auntie, and the word 'be' facing both ways gives BE plus EB, so the clue spells out the broadcaster's nickname Auntie Beeb

explanation.surface: An elderly aunt who cannot make up her mind which way to look.
explanation.walkthrough: The British broadcaster is affectionately called 'Auntie' or 'Auntie Beeb'; BEEB is 'be' written forwards and then backwards. The answer runs across four lights.
explanation.definitionFit: Auntie Beeb is the long-standing affectionate nickname of the national public broadcaster in Britain.

clue.text: Beast of former years entering craft

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other, as the dates go into the vessel

parts.note: a boat is a craft
BC, before Christ, labels dates of years long past

explanation.surface: An ancient animal climbing aboard a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A bobcat is a North American wild cat, a kind of wild animal.

clue.text: My tears are a river — it's the pressure

parts.note: if I weep, I sob, so 'my tears' gives I SOB

explanation.surface: Someone's weeping so hard they fill a river and blame the stress.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is a line on a weather map joining places of equal atmospheric pressure, so it stands for the pressure shown there.

clue.text: Not nice point about railroad

indicators.note: about means around, so the point verb surrounds the railway

parts.note: to point is to indicate
EL is the American elevated railroad

explanation.surface: An impolite gesture made towards a railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: EL, short for elevated railroad, is an Americanism for an overhead city railway such as Chicago's.
explanation.definitionFit: Indelicate means lacking tact or refinement, which is to say not nice.

clue.text: Beast has joint on order

parts.note: the hip is a joint
PO is a postal order, a British money order bought at a post office

explanation.surface: An animal with a hip joint being ordered about.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the joint above the order.
explanation.definitionFit: A hippo, short for hippopotamus, is a large African animal.

clue.text: See 1
Chorus to a work of Sellar and Yeatman, say

indicators.note: to work something is to knead or rework it, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A chorus added to a book by the authors of the comic history 1066 and All That.
explanation.walkthrough: W. C. Sellar and R. J. Yeatman jointly wrote 1066 and All That, a classic British parody of school history; 'work' looks like a noun but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sellar and Yeatman wrote their book together, making each an example of a joint writer of one work.

clue.text: Gentle revolution in aeronautics?

parts.note: not a quiet political upheaval in the aircraft industry but an unhurried turn of a plane through a full circle about its long axis

explanation.surface: A peaceful upheaval in the world of aircraft design.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow roll is an aerobatic manoeuvre in which an aircraft rotates steadily and gently about its longitudinal axis.

clue.text: Devil with legal authority going without saying

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
licit means permitted by law

explanation.surface: A demon armed with the law's blessing.
explanation.definitionFit: What is implicit is understood without being stated, so it goes without saying.

clue.text: Falsifying costume with heather

parts.note: garb is clothing or costume
ling is the common heather plant

explanation.surface: Faking a costume decorated with sprigs of heather.
explanation.definitionFit: Garbling a report distorts it, giving a false or muddled version.

clue.text: See 1
Noble, comprising a small coin and a penny, in thick fog

indicators.note: the noble holds the other pieces within, as something comprising them would

parts.note: a peer is a noble
a sou was a French coin of little value

explanation.surface: An aristocrat carrying a little loose change and lost in heavy fog.
explanation.definitionFit: A pea-souper is a dense yellowish London smog, named for its likeness to pea soup.

clue.text: A bolting lettuce, perhaps, on way back whatever happens

parts.note: a plant that bolts shoots up and grows tall
cos is a kind of lettuce, so the clue gives an example

indicators.note: back means the way abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: ST, street, is a way

explanation.surface: A lettuce running to seed beside the road, whatever comes of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bolting' suggests running away, but here it is the gardener's sense of a plant shooting up.
explanation.definitionFit: At all costs is an idiom meaning regardless of the price, so whatever happens.

clue.text: See 19
What beast and craftsman discussed on beach (it doesn't say what in the text)

definitions.text: What beast and craftsman discussed on beach (it doesn't say what in the text)

parts.words: What beast and craftsman discussed on beach (it doesn't say what in the text)
parts.note: the beast and craftsman are Lewis Carroll's Walrus and Carpenter, who on the sand say the time has come to talk of a long unspecified list of topics

explanation.surface: A question about an animal and a tradesman chatting at the seaside, with a coy aside.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass the Walrus announces the time has come 'to talk of many things: of shoes and ships and sealing-wax'; the bracket jokes that the poem never says which.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the Walrus's own vague summary of their talk, quoted from Carroll's poem.

clue.text: See 1
Books holiday in areas with securities for shrubs

indicators.note: in places the books and holiday inside the areas

parts.note: a rod, or square rod, is an old unit of land area
OT, the Old Testament, is a set of books
hol is short for holiday

explanation.surface: Reading books on holiday in various regions while holding securities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Securities' looks financial but means things that hold fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Rootholds are the anchorages that roots grip, securing plants such as shrubs in place.

clue.text: Top university with everyday story scene

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the university loses its first letter

parts.note: Cambridge is a university

explanation.surface: A leading university providing the setting for an ordinary tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archers, a long-running BBC radio soap, was billed as 'an everyday story of country folk' and is set in the village of Ambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambridge is the fictional village where the radio serial billed as an everyday story of country folk takes place.

parts.note: the answer to 25 across read as two words is digital in, and the blank completes the matching slogan of the TV switchover with its opposite

explanation.surface: A slogan with one word missing, cross-referring to another answer.
explanation.walkthrough: When British television switched from old to digital broadcasting, the catchphrase was the old signal out and the new one in.
explanation.definitionFit: Analogue is the opposite of digital, the older signal switched off as digital came in.

clue.text: Battle with Homeric objective grips America last of all, in outrageous fashion

parts.note: Mons in Belgium was a First World War battle

indicators.note: grips means the city holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: Troy was the city the Greeks besieged in Homer's Iliad
US is America

indicators.note: last of means only the final letter of the following word is taken

explanation.surface: A warrior aiming at Troy holds America above all in an outrageous way.
explanation.definitionFit: Monstrously means shockingly or outrageously, describing how something is done.

clue.text: Arithmetician's greeting to students of pioneer school

parts.note: a summer is one who sums, an arithmetician
hi is a greeting
L is a learner driver, so LL is students

explanation.surface: A mathematician waves hello to pupils at a progressive school.
explanation.walkthrough: Summerhill is the progressive Suffolk boarding school founded by A. S. Neill, a pioneer of free schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: Summerhill was a pioneering free school where children chose whether to attend lessons.

clue.text: Fashion models not on high frequency

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape, so the letters of the word are reshaped

explanation.surface: Fashion models rarely appear on the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High frequency' looks like a radio band but simply means often.
explanation.definitionFit: Seldom means rarely, which is to say not often or not with high frequency.

clue.text: See 6
America's late guide to viewers and listeners?

definitions.meaning: the US president's residence stands for American government, as in 'America's position'

definitions.text: late guide to viewers and listeners?
definitions.meaning: the late Mary ... campaigned on standards in broadcasting through her National Viewers' and Listeners' Association

explanation.surface: An American who used to steer television and radio audiences.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Whitehouse was a British campaigner against sex and violence on BBC television; the question mark marks the playful sense of 'guide'.
explanation.definitionFit: The official residence of the president is used to mean the American administration, and the surname belongs to the late broadcasting campaigner.

clue.text: Number with alternative, of course

parts.note: ten is a number
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A figure with an option, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally', but 'of' is a link and 'course' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenor means the general course or drift, as in the tenor of a conversation.

clue.text: Halo then for the old hovel?

parts.note: a halo marks a saint, abbreviated ST
ye is an old spelling of the, as in ye olde shoppe

explanation.surface: A halo found long ago in a shabby dwelling.
explanation.walkthrough: STYE is an old spelling of sty, a pig's pen or squalid dwelling; the question mark flags the archaic form.
explanation.definitionFit: A sty is a filthy pen or wretched dwelling, so a hovel.

clue.text: Stimulant to archaeological work not altogether from Italy

parts.note: a dig is an archaeological excavation

indicators.note: not altogether means the word is incomplete, missing one letter

parts.note: from Italy means Italian

explanation.surface: A drug that helps excavators, imported partly from Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Digitalin, extracted from foxglove, stimulates the heart muscle.

clue.text: Wandering? On the contrary, worse than that

definitions.note: the clue's adjective is matched by the noun used attributively, as in a nomad life

parts.note: no contradicts what was said
worse than a wandering mind is being mad

explanation.surface: Someone protests they are not merely absent-minded but worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering' first suggests a straying mind, and the clue plays on that: worse than wandering wits is MAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad roams from place to place with no fixed home, a wanderer.

clue.text: Champs Elyseé no see?

indicators.note: champs is a verb meaning chews, so the word that follows is mangled

parts.note: the second word of the Paris avenue's name in full, with the final S the printed word lacks

explanation.surface: Strolling the famous Paris avenue but unable to see anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champs' looks like part of the avenue's name but is the chewing signal; the fodder must be ELYSEES, the avenue's full second word, to give seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeless means without eyes, and so unable to see.

clue.text: Play casually following Roundhead round platform

indicators.note: following places the strumming after the other pieces

parts.note: the head of the word round is its first letter R
O is round in shape
to strum is to play a guitar idly

explanation.surface: A Cromwellian soldier idly playing a tune on a stage.
explanation.walkthrough: A Roundhead was a Parliamentarian in the English Civil War; here it is read as the head of round.
explanation.definitionFit: A rostrum is a raised platform for a speaker or conductor.
